extracted.intended_audience: research funders, grant administrators, policy-makers and researchers studying peer review and research funding
extracted.subtask_description: A literature-review style synthesis of evidence about the effectiveness, biases, burden, timeliness and possible reforms of grant peer review systems aimed at informing funders and policy-makers. Covers empirical findings and recommended interventions (blinding, triage, lotteries, shortened applications, reviewer training, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias against innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is strong evidence that peer review is biased against innovative research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report highlights this as the strongest bias found and recommends portfolio approaches that explicitly include innovation, measuring reviewer disagreement as a possible indicator of innovation, and experimental evaluation of interventions to counter this bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence on gender bias in grant peer review is conflicting: some studies (e.g. Wenneras & Wold; Bornmann et al.) report lower success rates for women (men ~7% more likely in a meta-analysis), while other reviews find no systematic bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The literature is mixed and sensitive to aggregation and cohort effects; funders should consider context, longitudinal changes, and careful modeling when assessing gender effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age bias / early career disadvantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns that review processes relying on prior publications/funding may disadvantage early career researchers; studies show mixed findings with some indicating declines in success with age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders (e.g. NIH) have introduced measures to equalise success rates between new and established investigators for new applications; eligibility and targeted policy can address structural causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional prestige / departmental bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers may favour proposals from particular departments, senior researchers, or those already academically recognised, producing bias related to institutional prestige.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blinding/anonymisation of proposals is sometimes used to mitigate this, though feasibility and effectiveness are debated; evidence shows only weak correlation between blinded short versions and unblinded full proposals in some studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cronyism and conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior affiliation with reviewers or panel members can increase funding chances; panel members may also personally benefit (submit more applications/get more awards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major funders use detailed conflict-of-interest procedures; separating genuine expertise effects from nepotism is challenging and requires careful policy and monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive particularism / intellectual distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers tend to favour work in their own intellectual tradition or field ('cognitive particularism'), though some evidence shows reviewers may favour areas they are very familiar with or completely unfamiliar with; other studies find reviewers are more critical in their own expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel composition should balance specialist expertise with broader appreciation; funders should be cautious in interpreting apparent bias since specialist expertise also improves assessment accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary field effects (field bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain fields (e.g. molecular biology) appear statistically more likely to receive funding than other bioscience fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders could broaden the range of scientific problems judged by each group or ensure field-diverse panels to counter overvaluation of particular fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review processes can be slow (commonly 9–18 months from submission to funding), which may slow scientific progress or reduce timeliness of responses to emergencies (e.g. epidemics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider streamlined processes, shorter applications, rapid pathways for time-critical research, and measure the impact of review timelines on translation and economic viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant-side burden is substantial (estimates indicate ~74–85% of monetised burden lies in application production), with high time and stress costs and significant institutional workload.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority should be given to reducing applicant burden or increasing the value to unsuccessful applicants (e.g. better feedback); proposals to shorten forms must be carefully evaluated because shorter forms do not always reduce preparation time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on reviewers and panel members
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer and panel time is a significant cost (often ~15% of burden); organisations report increasing difficulty recruiting senior reviewers and increased decline/late reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies trial simplified review processes (shortened applications, smaller panels) that saved substantial review costs and achieved acceptable agreement levels; optimizing reviewer numbers balances reproducibility and burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application length and complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Lengthy and complex applications (e.g. 80–120 pages) increase burden. Some funders shortened applications (NIH R01 from 25 to 12 pages) but evidence on impact is mixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reductions in length/complexity should be evaluated experimentally; earlier studies show mixed effects on preparation time and success rates, so careful piloting is advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triage / short preliminary applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Using short preliminary applications with triage (e.g. NSF introduced triage with ~75% cull rate) can reduce administrative burden and reviewer workload.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While praised for reducing burden, simultaneous policy changes can confound evaluation; funders should monitor effects on success rates and application volumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimal number of reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical work suggests trade-offs between reproducibility and reviewer burden; one study found five reviewers optimal, another found 11 reviewers most effective in a different scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The optimal number depends on the scheme and desired balance between reproducibility and cost; funders should use modelling and empirical testing to choose reviewer counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymisation / blinding of reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Blinding reviewers to applicant identity is used by some funders to reduce bias, but its feasibility and effectiveness are disputed because anonymisation may be imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement blinding with caution; evaluate empirically since some studies find only weak correlations between blinded short and unblinded full assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer training to address bias and improve quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Training approaches have been used (e.g. CIHR, NIH) to address bias and improve review quality, with limited evidence that they reduce discrepancies between reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders may deploy training but should rigorously evaluate its effectiveness in reducing bias and improving assessment consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture reviewer uncertainty and disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review uncertainty is substantial and often unacknowledged; reviewers should be asked for both ratings and a measure of confidence, and disagreement may be informative (e.g. indicating innovation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders should record confidence levels, analyse disagreement patterns, and use these metrics to inform portfolio decisions and interpretation of scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce randomness / lottery mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Random allocation (lottery) within a fundable pool or two-threshold systems (fund above high threshold, reject below low threshold, randomise between) are proposed to address low reliability of fine-grained decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lotteries can reduce selection bias from marginal decisions and have been trialled in limited cases (e.g. New Zealand Explorer Grants); political acceptability and eligibility criteria need careful design and empirical testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel composition diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Broaden the range of scientific fields and include diverse expertise on panels to counter specialist overvaluation and cognitive particularism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include senior scientists with wide appreciation of different fields to counteract specialists' tendency to overvalue work in their own field, while weighing the benefits of specialist assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Face-to-face vs remote panel discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Remote/technology-enabled review can reduce travel time and burden and does not appear to significantly affect outcomes, but face-to-face meetings provide social interactions and network benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders should consider trade-offs between cost/time savings and social/interactive benefits of in-person panels; alternative supports may be needed if remote review reduces valuable side-benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide value to applicants (feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: Making the application process more valuable to applicants (e.g. through substantive reviewer and panel feedback) could offset applicant burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders should explore enhancing feedback quality and consider non-financial benefits as part of burden-reduction strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use technology to reduce administrative and time burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology (e.g. remote meetings, online systems) can reduce time and administrative burden for panel members and funders without markedly changing outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt appropriate technology solutions while monitoring effects on review quality and social processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility and consistency of review decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: There is evidence of inconsistency and weak reproducibility in peer review ratings and panel decisions; lack of an absolute standard makes assessment difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders should acknowledge uncertainty, measure reproducibility, and avoid over-reliance on single scores; consider multi-criteria and portfolio approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive validity for future performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review scores show weak predictive power for future bibliometric or academic performance in many studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders should be cautious about interpreting scores as predictors of long-term impact and consider complementary metrics and follow-up evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve the evidence base: publish, evaluate and share data
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a lack of robust comparative evidence on peer review interventions because funders seldom publish internal evaluations; better evidence is needed on effectiveness and system-level impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders should build before-and-after comparisons into changes, make data available for analysis, publish evaluations, and cooperate on comparative studies despite sensitivity around allocation procedures.
